notes.title: Poisson Distribution — Epistemic Tool

headings.text: Treating λ as a property of the world

notes.text: poisson distribution — epistemic tool episte cnica catalog ◐ light poisson distribution identity formal simulation validation scope identity formal simulation validation scope epistemic tool analysis poisson distribution a discrete probability distribution that transforms observations of rare event counts into probabilistic claims about reality's rate structure. 01 identity name poisson distribution named after siméon denis poisson (1837) type generative / inferential belongs to the class of probability models — tools that encode uncertainty about observables through parametric structures. one-line summary maps a rate parameter λ to a probability distribution over non-negative integer counts, assuming events occur independently at constant average rate. epistemic insight the poisson distribution is not merely a formula — it is a compression device that reduces infinite possible temporal event patterns into a single scalar λ, preserving only the rate information while discarding all temporal structure. 02 formal characterization probability mass function p(x = k) = e -λ · λ k / k! λ rate parameter (expected count) k observed count (k ∈ {0, 1, 2, ...}) e euler's number (~2.718) input space single positive real number λ ∈ ℝ⁺ representing the expected number of events per unit interval (time, space, etc.) output space probability distribution over non-negative integers ℤ⁺₀ with infinite but countable support. transformation t: ℝ⁺ → δ(ℤ⁺₀) maps rate to probability distribution over counts. interactive pmf λ = k (count) mean: 4 | variance: 4 | mode: 3, 4 key properties mean (e[x]) λ variance (var(x)) λ equidispersion e[x] = var(x) skewness 1/√λ mode ⌊λ⌋ and ⌈λ⌉ - 1 additive property if x₁ ~ poisson(λ₁) and x₂ ~ poisson(λ₂) are independent: x₁ + x₂ ~ poisson(λ₁ + λ₂) this property enables aggregation of counts across intervals while preserving distributional form. 03 assumptions & preconditions stationarity the rate λ remains constant throughout the observation period. event probability does not change over time or space. required independence the occurrence of one event does not affect the probability of another. no clustering or contagion effects. required rarity (at infinitesimal scale) in very small subintervals, the probability of more than one event is negligible. events occur one at a time. required epistemic warning these assumptions are rarely perfectly satisfied in real-world data. the poisson distribution is best understood as an idealization — a useful approximation whose validity must be assessed, not assumed. 04 mechanism & simulation observe how poisson-distributed events emerge from a constant-rate process. each simulation generates events over time intervals, demonstrating the relationship between λ and observed counts. rate (λ events/unit time) 1 5 15 intervals 5 20 50 run simulation event timeline each dot represents an event occurrence over time count distribution count (k) sample mean: — law of large numbers observe sample mean converging to λ as observations accumulate reset sample size (n) |sample mean - λ|: — 05 epistemic role function the poisson distribution resolves the epistemic gap between: → observing discrete counts and needing probabilistic predictions → summarizing rate information while quantifying uncertainty → enabling inference from partial observations to population parameters preservation profile expected count — λ is preserved as both mean and variance additivity — counts can be summed while preserving distribution independence structure — assumed and propagated forward destruction / loss profile × temporal structure — when events occurred is lost × event characteristics — magnitude, duration, severity × causal dependencies — why events occurred × rate variation — fluctuations in λ over time × overdispersion — variance exceeding mean × zero-inflation — excess zeros beyond model 06 validation & failure modes correctness empirical failures formal correctness criteria limit theorem poisson arises as limit of binomial(n, p) as n → ∞, p → 0, np → λ. this provides mathematical grounding for the "rare events" interpretation. maximum entropy among all distributions with fixed mean on non-negative integers, poisson has maximum entropy. it makes minimal additional assumptions. consistency the sample mean converges to λ almost surely (slln), providing consistent estimation. empirical validation methods dispersion test check if variance ≈ mean (equidispersion holds) sample mean sample variance test chi-square goodness of fit compare observed frequencies with expected frequencies under poisson model. systematic failure modes overdispersion when variance > mean. common in clustered data, mixed populations, or when independence fails. alternative: negative binomial underdispersion when variance alternative: generalized poisson, com-poisson zero-inflation excess zeros beyond what poisson predicts. common in "hurdle" scenarios or structural zeros. alternative: zero-inflated poisson (zip) 07 scope & limits valid domains • radioactive decay events • phone calls at a call center • website hits per minute • typographical errors per page • mutations in dna sequences • arrivals at a queue questionable domains • disease outbreaks (contagion) • traffic accidents (clustering) • insurance claims (catastrophes) • crime statistics (hot spots) • ecological counts (aggregation) structural limits • cannot model bimodality • single parameter limits flexibility • requires constant rate • no memory of past events • integer-only support comparative position tool parameters variance/mean when to use poisson λ = 1 rare, independent events binomial n, p < 1 fixed number of trials negative binomial r, p > 1 overdispersed counts geometric p > 1 waiting time until success 08 diagnostic questions what happens if the rate λ varies over time? if the rate varies, you're no longer dealing with a single poisson process. the aggregate will typically show overdispersion — variance exceeds mean. this is because: var(total) = e[var(x|λ)] + var(e[x|λ]) = e[λ] + var(λ) > e[λ] the mixture of poissons with varying λ creates a compound distribution with greater spread. can two different processes produce indistinguishable count distributions? yes. this is an identifiability problem. given only count data, you cannot distinguish between: a homogeneous poisson process with rate λ a mixture of poisson processes with varying rates averaging to λ a process with clustered arrivals that happen to match the count distribution the count distribution alone is insufficient to recover the underlying process structure. what invariant does poisson rely on most critically? the equidispersion invariant : e[x] = var(x). this is the signature property that distinguishes poisson from other count distributions. when this invariant fails: overdispersion → model underestimates variability underdispersion → model overestimates variability checking this invariant is the first diagnostic for poisson appropriateness. how does sample size affect poisson inference? with larger samples: estimate precision improves (∝ 1/√n) but assumption violations become more detectable small departures from poisson become statistically significant paradoxically, large samples can make poisson less applicable — not because the model is more wrong, but because you can detect smaller departures from it. 09 cognitive friction systematic misunderstandings confusion between artifact and reality the poisson distribution describes our representation of uncertainty, not the underlying generative process. real events don't "follow" a poisson — our model assumes independence and constant rate as useful approximations. misinterpretation of assumptions as facts independence and stationarity are assumed , not discovered. they are simplifying choices that make the model tractable, not empirical truths to be accepted uncritically. overextension beyond scope applying poisson to bounded counts (can't exceed n), heavy-tailed phenomena (power law distributions), or clustered data violates core assumptions. the model's simplicity invites overuse. treating λ as a property of the world λ is an epistemic parameter — a summary of our expectations — not an ontological feature. different observers with different information may legitimately use different λ values for the same phenomenon. tool poisson distribution type probability model / generative created interactive epistemic notebook episte cnica · notes ← catalog

notes.title: Standard Deviation — Epistemic Notebook
notes.text: standard deviation — epistemic notebook episte cnica catalog ◐ light epistemic notebook identity formal mechanism playground limits tool specification standard deviation a measure of dispersion that quantifies how much individual observations deviate from the central tendency — encoding uncertainty about the typical value. 01 identity type classification compressive / diagnostic standard deviation belongs to the class of descriptive statistics — it compresses a distribution of values into a single scalar that characterizes spread, enabling diagnostic assessment of data homogeneity. one-line summary σ = √(σ(xᵢ - μ)² / n) transforms a collection of observations into a single scalar representing the root-mean-square deviation from the arithmetic mean — quantifying the "typical distance" of points from center. epistemic role resolves uncertainty about the reliability of the mean as a representative value. without dispersion measures, central tendency is epistemically incomplete. preserves relative ordering of distances, magnitude relationships, and (crucially) the same units as the original data — enabling direct interpretation. destroys direction of deviations (always positive), distribution shape (skew, modality), individual observation positions, and temporal ordering. 02 formal characterization transformation mapping 𝒯 : ℝⁿ → ℝ₊ | (x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ) ↦ σ input space (𝒜ᵢₙ) → a finite set of n real-valued observations → measurements on an interval or ratio scale → no requirement on distribution shape output space (𝒜ₒᵤₜ) ← a single non-negative real number ← in the same units as input observations ← bounded: σ = 0 iff all values identical computational decomposition interact with each step to observe the transformation pipeline. click on data points to modify the input. step 1 xᵢ raw data step 2 μ = σxᵢ/n mean step 3 (xᵢ - μ) deviations step 4 (xᵢ - μ)² squared diffs step 5 σ = √(σ/n) result reset randomize n = 8 μ = 0.00 σ = 0.00 03 mechanism constituent 1 arithmetic mean the centroid of the data — the point that minimizes the sum of squared deviations. sd is meaningless without this reference point. constituent 2 squared deviation squaring achieves two goals: it removes sign (direction) and disproportionately penalizes larger deviations — making sd sensitive to outliers. constituent 3 square root returns the measure to original units, enabling direct interpretation. without it, we would have variance (σ²) which is harder to interpret. outlier sensitivity analysis drag the outlier point to observe how standard deviation responds compared to other measures. note the quadratic sensitivity to extreme values. outlier position sd 1.00 mad 0.74 iqr 1.35 04 interactive playground distribution builder click on the canvas to add points. observe how sd changes with distribution shape. clear all σ = — distribution comparison adjust spread to compare identical means with different dispersions. low σ 1.0 high σ 3.0 normal distribution & the 68-95-99.7 rule for normally distributed data, standard deviation defines probability intervals. adjust σ to see how coverage changes. ±1σ ±2σ ±3σ standard deviation (σ) 1.0 mean (μ) 50 coverage intervals μ ± 1σ contains: 68.27% μ ± 2σ contains: 95.45% μ ± 3σ contains: 99.73% 05 sample vs population bessel's correction when estimating population sd from a sample, dividing by (n-1) instead of n produces an unbiased estimator . this correction accounts for the fact that sample variance systematically underestimates population variance. population sd σ = √(σ(xᵢ - μ)² / n) sample sd (corrected) s = √(σ(xᵢ - x̄)² / (n-1)) apply bessel's correction convergence demo observe how sample sd approaches population sd as sample size increases. the correction matters most for small samples. n = 10 resample 06 scope & limits scope of applicability ● interval or ratio scale data (meaningful distances) ● unimodal, approximately symmetric distributions ● contexts where outliers represent measurement error ● comparing variability across datasets with similar units structural limitations ● not applicable to nominal or ordinal data ● misleading for multimodal distributions ● cannot distinguish between different shapes with same spread ● exponentially sensitive to outliers (non-robust) failure mode simulator select a distribution type to see where standard deviation fails to capture the true structure of the data. bimodal skewed contaminated uniform the problem in a bimodal distribution, the mean falls between the two modes — a region with few or no observations. the standard deviation then measures spread around this meaningless central point, capturing neither the spread within each cluster nor the distance between clusters. better alternatives • report modes and their locations • use iqr or mad for robust spread • apply mixture model decomposition current distribution σ = 2.12 | mad = 1.48 07 diagnostic questions what happens if assumptions are violated? standard deviation remains mathematically computable for any set of real numbers. however, its epistemic meaning degrades: • skewed data: sd is pulled toward the tail, overstating "typical" spread • multimodal data: the mean is not representative, making sd meaningless • heavy tails: sd understates extreme event probability • outliers: single values can arbitrarily inflate sd what invariant does this tool rely on most critically? the assumption that the arithmetic mean is a meaningful center . this requires: • unimodal or symmetric distribution • data measured on interval/ratio scale • no extreme asymmetry in the underlying process without this, sd measures spread around a point that doesn't represent the data's central tendency. can different distributions produce the same sd? yes — infinitely many. this is a core limitation: sd is a lossy compression. examples with identical mean and sd: • normal distribution vs uniform distribution • bimodal vs unimodal distributions • symmetric vs moderately skewed distributions this is why sd should always be accompanied by visualization or additional measures. why square the deviations instead of using absolute values? squaring has both practical and theoretical justifications: • mathematical convenience: squared functions are differentiable everywhere • optimal estimation: mean minimizes sum of squared errors • theoretical foundations: central limit theorem involves variance • penalization: larger deviations are disproportionately weighted the alternative — mean absolute deviation (mad) — is more robust but has less convenient mathematical properties. 08 comparative position measure robustness efficiency interpretability when to use sd (σ) low high (normal) high symmetric, clean data; statistical inference mad high low (normal) medium data with outliers; quick robustness check iqr high medium medium skewed data; box plots; outlier detection variance (σ²) low high low theoretical work; additive decomposition epistemic notebook series standard deviation v1.0 episte cnica · notes ← catalog

⏳ waiting on id= accounts table · data, per-txn views & locks row committed t1 sees t2 sees held locks wait queue — — s shared (read) x exclusive (write) w waiting in queue pending (uncommitted) writes shown per-txn in the “sees” columns. timeline · interleaved history no operations yet. issue begin on t1 or t2, then try an update. # how this simulator works (click to expand) model. each transaction follows strict two-phase locking : it acquires locks while running and releases them all only at commit or rollback. locks. select takes an s (shared) lock; select for update , update , delete and insert take an x (exclusive) lock. two s locks coexist; an x lock is incompatible with anything else. a transaction that already holds s may upgrade to x if it is the sole holder. blocking. if a requested lock conflicts, the transaction goes waiting and is queued on that row. when the holder releases (commit/rollback), the queue head is re-granted automatically. deadlocks. after every lock wait, a wait-for graph is checked for cycles. if a cycle is found, the transaction that just closed the cycle is chosen as the victim and rolled back — the alert shows the cycle. programs & stepping. each transaction holds a multi-statement program (one sql statement per line). use step t1 / step t2 to advance one statement at a time — you control the interleaving , which is how deadlocks and races are produced. a statement that blocks pauses the program counter (▶); when its lock is later granted (e.g. the other transaction commits), it resumes automatically and the counter advances. rewind aborts and resets a transaction to its first statement. isolation you can observe. the “sees” columns show each transaction’s own view: it reads its own pending writes, otherwise the committed value. notice a writer’s pending value is invisible to the other transaction until commit. sql. the text box accepts a small subset: begin , commit , rollback , select ... where id=n [for update] , update t set col = v where id=n , update t set col = col +/- v where id=n , delete from t where id=n , insert into t values (v) . episte cnica · notes ← catalog
